extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy, aesthetics, and art theory
extracted.subtask_description: Philosophical exposition of genius, imagination, aesthetic contemplation, the beautiful and the sublime, and the relation of genius to madness; intended to articulate the mental capacities and states that produce artistic creation and aesthetic pleasure. Useful for analyzing or teaching theories of art and aesthetic experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extraordinary strength of imagination (necessary but not sufficient for genius)
rubrics_metrics.description: Extraordinary strength of imagination accompanies, and is indeed a necessary condition of genius. But the converse does not hold, for strength of imagination does not indicate genius.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imagination must extend the intellectual horizon beyond present objects and enable construction of wholes from limited perception. Anti-pattern: strong imagination merely used for private fantasising ('building castles in the air') yields dreamers and popular novelists rather than genius.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge of Ideas independent of the principle of sufficient reason
rubrics_metrics.description: Genius consists in the capacity for knowing, independently of the principle of sufficient reason, not individual things in their relations but the Ideas of such things (the enduring form of the species).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This kind of knowledge allows the genius to apprehend a particular as representative of its whole species. It contrasts with ordinary cognition, which seeks relations and is governed by causality and motivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disinterested, will-less contemplation as distinctive cognitive mode
rubrics_metrics.description: The man of genius can direct attention to objects 'wholly disinterested' — purely objective perception free from relation to his will — enabling pure knowing rather than knowledge directed by motives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ordinary persons perceive only insofar as things relate to their will and quickly seek concepts useful to life; geniuses linger in perception and attain aesthetic knowledge. Failure to detach from will is a key deficiency in ordinary cognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: External expression of genius: predominance of knowledge over will
rubrics_metrics.description: The expression of genius in a face consists in a decided predominance of knowledge over will, visible as a keen and steady glance — 'pure knowing' rather than the expression of will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an observable sign distinguishing men of genius from ordinary mortals, whose countenances commonly express will and practical concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imagination must abstract from imperfect actual objects to the Idea
rubrics_metrics.description: Actual objects are almost always imperfect copies of the Ideas expressed in them; therefore the man of genius requires imagination in order to see in things not what Nature has actually made, but what she endeavoured to make.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Artistic production involves abstracting the Idea from the actual and omitting disturbing accidents; the artist 'lets us see the world through his eyes' by reproducing the Idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Antagonism between genius and mathematical/logical method
rubrics_metrics.description: The disinclination of men of genius to mathematics: mathematical and strictly logical methods, being bound to universal forms of space and time and memory, are antagonistic to the perceptive method of genius and may obstruct true insight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically observed examples: Goethe's alleged want of mathematical knowledge; conversely, admirable mathematicians often have little susceptibility for the fine arts. This is an explanatory criterion, not a strict exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mutual exclusion of prudence (sagacity) and genius while active
rubrics_metrics.description: Quick comprehension of relations in accordance with laws of causality and motivation (prudence) is what constitutes sagacity; this mode is opposed to the perception-of-Ideas that constitutes genius, so a prudent man, so far as he is prudent, will not be a genius, and vice versa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a person is operating in the genius mode (pure perception), the dispositions that produce prudential, relational thinking are sidelined; expect eccentricity and impractical action as consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propensity of genius toward violent emotions and irrational passions
rubrics_metrics.description: Persons of genius are often subject to violent emotions and irrational passions, not from weakness of reason but from preponderance of perceptive (Idea) knowledge over abstract reason, producing a tendency to the perceptible and to impulsive action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This explains familiar biographical patterns (e.g., Rousseau, Byron) and literary portrayals (Goethe's Torquato Tasso). It is presented as a typical correlate, not a necessary pathology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation between genius and madness (similarities and distinctions)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a direct connection between genius and madness: both can neglect the continuity of relations and memory, and both may display extremes; yet they differ — delirium falsifies perception, madness falsifies thoughts (especially relations to past), while genius achieves true knowledge of Ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Madness is characterized by broken continuity of memory and false pasts (monomania, folly), whereas genius's neglect of relations arises from focusing on Ideas. Biographical and asylum observations support a non-coincidental correlation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Madness primarily concerns discontinuity of memory and false relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Madmen often perceive the immediate present correctly but err in knowledge of the absent and past; their thread of memory is broken and they fill gaps with fictions, producing fixed or momentary false ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This account distinguishes types (monomania, melancholy, folly) and explains how great suffering can precipitate such a breakdown as a 'last resource' to escape unbearable memory-laden pain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genius's tendency to see extremes and lack the mean
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the particular perceived by genius is raised to the fullness of its Idea, geniuses often see extremes and cannot hit the mean — their actions tend to extremes and lack soberness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequently geniuses may be easily deceived in matters of individuals and practical affairs, and may be 'a tool in the hands of the crafty.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Art as means to communicate Ideas by abstracting from the actual
rubrics_metrics.description: The work of art is a means of facilitating the knowledge of the Idea: the artist, who knows the Idea rather than the actual, reproduces the pure Idea in his work by omitting disturbing accidents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Art's technical side is the acquired skill enabling the artist to lend others his perceptual access to Ideas; successful art presents the Idea more readily than nature itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic contemplation consists of two inseparable parts
rubrics_metrics.description: In the æsthetical mode of contemplation there are two inseparable constituent parts — (1) the knowledge of the object as Idea (not as individual), and (2) the self-consciousness of the knowing person as pure will-less subject of knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both must appear united for true aesthetic pleasure; the balance between them varies with objects and explains different aesthetic responses (beautiful vs. sublime).

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic pleasure arises from release of knowledge from service of the will
rubrics_metrics.description: All willing arises from want; when some external cause or inward disposition lifts us out of willing and delivers knowledge from the slavery of the will, we achieve pure will-less knowing and experience a painless peace — the basis of aesthetic pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This explains why nature or art can suddenly calm passionate persons: by enabling disinterested contemplation. The state is transient and ends when any relation to will returns to consciousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty: objects that readily present their Ideas ('bend themselves' to perception)
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauty (in the objective sense) consists in the fittingness of objects whose manifold yet definite and distinct form easily become representatives of their Ideas; such objects 'invite' æsthetic observation and afford æsthetic satisfaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Natural beauty and certain painted subjects (still life, certain landscapes) are particularly effective because they facilitate pure perception. The artist's role can be to present such forms to the beholder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensorial hierarchy for aesthetic valuation (vision and light privileged)
rubrics_metrics.description: Light and sight are the most gladdening and are correlative of the most perfect kind of perceptive knowledge (least connected to the will); colours and transparency excite keen delight. Smell and taste are most closely related to the will and are therefore 'the most ignoble' senses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aesthetic preference and delight often derive from the capacity for pure perceptive knowledge provided by vision/light (e.g., reflections in water). This provides a criterion for why certain sensory modalities yield higher aesthetic pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artistic technique that facilitates objective perception (still life, landscape)
rubrics_metrics.description: Works such as Dutch still life and certain landscapes achieve and express the artist's purely objective perception by directing attention to 'insignificant' objects and enabling viewers to participate in the same peaceful, will-less frame of mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such art increases the onlooker's emotion especially when contrasted with the spectator's usual disturbed will-bound state; this is an example of how form and subject matter can be chosen to promote aesthetic contemplation.
